image.altEn: Spanish-language xkcd comic #664: Academia vs. Business

titleText.es: Algún ingeniero de por ahí ha resuelto el problema P=NP y está enzarzado en una rutina de calibración de una batidora eléctrica. Por cada 0x5f375a86 que descubrimos, hay miles que no vemos.
titleText.en: Some engineer out there has solved P=NP and it's locked up in an electric eggbeater calibration routine.  For every 0x5f375a86 we learn about, there are thousands we never see.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive and official xkcd source both identify comic #664. The Spanish title text translates the official examples of important discoveries hidden in routine engineering. The raster supplies both large branch bubbles that OCR missed, joins the line-broken PÁRRAFO, and keeps 48, 200, and OUTLOOK as nonlexical source units.

regions.labelEs: ACABO DE ESCRIBIR EL CÓDIGO MÁS BONITO DE MI VIDA.

applications.explanationEn: Acabo changes for the speaker, de is the required link, and escribir remains in its unchanged -ir dictionary form.
El and código name the item being ranked, while más and bonito mark it as the highest degree of that description.

regions.labelEs: ME PASARON POR CASUALIDAD UN PROBLEMA IMPOSIBLE. EN 48 HORAS Y 200 LÍNEAS, LO HE RESUELTO.

excludedUnits.rationale: 48 is a numeral rather than a Spanish lexical word.
200 is a numeral rather than a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Por and casualidad work together as the conventional expression for an accidental or chance event.
He is the present helper for the speaker, and resuelto is resolver's irregular completed-action form.
Imposible follows problema because it gives a descriptive classification of the problem.
Imposible has one singular form for both masculine and feminine nouns, so it agrees with singular problema without changing its ending.

regions.labelEs: MUNDO ACADÉMICO — DIOS MÍO, ESTO SUPONDRÁ MEDIA DOCENA DE PAPERS, UNA O DOS TESIS Y UN PÁRRAFO EN TODOS LOS LIBROS DE TEXTO SOBRE TEORÍA DE COLAS.

applications.explanationEn: Dios and the following possessive mío form the conventional exclamation.
Media halves the quantity, docena names the dozen, and de introduces what is counted.
Libros carries the plural ending, while de texto stays fixed to classify the kind of books.
Académico follows mundo because it classifies the kind of world or sphere being named.
Académico uses masculine singular -o to match mundo.

regions.labelEs: MUNDO EMPRESARIAL — ¿HAS CONSEGUIDO QUE EL PROGRAMA DEJE DE IR LENTO? GENIAL. ¿PUEDES HACER QUE OUTLOOK SE SINCRONICE CON NUESTROS NUEVOS MÓVILES?

excludedUnits.rationale: Outlook is an unchanged software product name, not a Spanish lexical learning target.

applications.explanationEn: Empresarial follows mundo because it classifies the kind of world or sphere being named.
Empresarial has one singular form for both masculine and feminine nouns, so it agrees with singular mundo without changing its ending.
Has is the present helper for one familiar listener, and conseguido is conseguir's completed-action form.

applications.exampleEs: HAS CONSEGUIDO QUE EL PROGRAMA DEJE
applications.explanationEn: Has conseguido supplies the completed managed action, que introduces the other action, and deje is dejar's special caused-result form.
Deje changes to fit the managed result, de is the required link, and ir stays in its unchanged dictionary form as the action that stops.
Hacer que introduces the caused result, and sincronice is sincronizar's special caused-action form.
Nuestros takes masculine plural -os because it matches the masculine plural noun móviles.
Lento describes the slow manner of ir, so it stays in the fixed masculine singular form rather than agreeing with programa.
Nuevos comes before móviles to present the phones as newly added or recent, rather than emphasizing that they were newly manufactured.
Nuevos uses masculine plural -os to match móviles.

cards.answerEn: I have just (done something), as part of acabo de
cards.noteEn: Acabo is a form of acabar, which normally means “to finish.” When it is followed by de and an unchanged action verb, the three-part pattern says that the action happened just now.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an action happened just now?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of acabar, then de, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The final verb stays in its basic -ar, -er, or -ir form. Acabo de means “I have just,” acaba de means “he, she, or formal you has just,” and acabamos de means “we have just.” This pattern talks about recent time; it does not mean literally finishing the later action.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links acabar to a just-completed action
cards.noteEn: In acabar de plus an unchanged action verb, de is required even though natural English does not translate it separately.

cards.questionEn: How do you describe someone or something as the most of a quality?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of “the,” name the person or thing, then add más plus the describing word.
cards.noteEn: The opening el, la, los, or las agrees with the noun. Más stays unchanged, while the final adjective changes when Spanish normally requires agreement.

cards.questionEn: Why do the two workplaces react so differently to the same programming breakthrough?
cards.answerEn: The joke contrasts academic incentives to publish and teach a discovery with a company's narrow interest in whether its immediate software task now works.
cards.noteEn: The hidden breakthrough is treated as potentially important research in the academic branch, while the business branch evaluates it only as routine performance and compatibility work. The official title text sharpens the joke by suggesting that major theoretical discoveries may remain buried inside ordinary engineering code.
Más normally means “more.” After el, la, los, or las, it can instead mark the highest degree in a group: la más rápida means “the fastest one.”
Bonito can come before a noun when the speaker presents a positive, often personal evaluation. Its ending changes to match the noun: bonita, bonitos, or bonitas.

cards.answerEn: in; among (introducing what ‘best’ or ‘worst’ is compared across)
cards.noteEn: After a highest-or-lowest description such as el mejor or el peor, de can introduce the full group or time range being compared.

example.es: Es la mejor canción de la década.
example.en: It is the best song of the decade.

cards.noteEn: Pasaron is the completed-past they-form of pasar. With a recipient such as me and an object, pasar can mean to hand or give that object to someone.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins por casualidad
cards.noteEn: Por combines with casualidad to mean that something happened by chance.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happened by chance or unexpectedly?
cards.noteEn: Por stays fixed and casualidad names chance. The expression can modify an action directly or appear in questions where English might say “by any chance.”

example.en: I found the key by chance.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.answerEn: in; within (the time taken to finish)
cards.noteEn: Before a duration, en can state how much time an action took to complete.

example.es: Terminé el informe en dos horas.
example.en: I finished the report in two hours.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Resuelto is the irregular completed-action form of resolver; it appears with haber in forms such as he resuelto.

example.en: I have already solved the problem.

cards.noteEn: Dios names God, but said by itself it can also react to surprise, excitement, frustration, or strong nostalgia. The tone decides whether natural English keeps ‘God’ or uses an exclamation such as ‘man.’
Dios mío can express shock, frustration, or a literal address to God. Mío follows Dios and agrees with its masculine form.
Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.
Supondrá is the future form of suponer for one thing. Here it introduces the consequences something will bring.

example.en: The change will entail more work.

cards.noteEn: Media agrees with the feminine noun hora. Medio is used before a masculine noun.

cards.questionEn: How do you say approximately or exactly half a dozen of something?
cards.answerEn: Use media docena de, then name what is counted.
cards.noteEn: Media agrees with the feminine noun docena and means half. Docena stays singular here, and de introduces the counted thing; only the later noun normally changes for plural meaning.

example.en: We bought half a dozen eggs.

cards.answerEn: of; or no separate English word, linking an amount to what it measures
cards.noteEn: After a quantity expression, de introduces the substance or thing being measured. English uses “of” in expressions such as a lot of or the amount of, but may leave de untranslated in others, such as un poco de agua, “a little water.”

cards.answerEn: academic papers; research articles (informal English borrowing)
cards.noteEn: Spanish often prefers artículos or trabajos académicos. In academic conversation, the English borrowing paper is also used informally; its plural is papers.

example.en: She published two academic papers on astronomy.

cards.answerEn: one (feminine singular, before a counted noun)
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses un before a masculine noun and una before a feminine noun for both the number one and the indefinite article “a.” Context shows whether an exact count matters.
Tesis has the same written form in the singular and plural; surrounding words show the number.

example.es: Leyó dos tesis sobre el tema.
example.en: She read two theses on the topic.

cards.noteEn: Libros is the masculine plural of libro.

cards.questionEn: What common Spanish phrase means a textbook?
cards.answerEn: Use libro de texto; use libros de texto for more than one.
cards.noteEn: Libro is the main noun and carries the plural ending. De texto classifies the book's use and stays unchanged in the plural.

example.es: Necesito un libro de texto nuevo.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to its type
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”
In teoría de colas, colas are mathematical waiting lines studied in systems where jobs or people wait for service.

example.es: La teoría de colas ayuda a modelar esperas.
example.en: Queueing theory helps model waiting times.

cards.promptEs: conseguir que + otra persona o cosa + verbo en subjuntivo
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone manages to get another person or thing to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of conseguir, then que, then the other actor's action in the special subjunctive form.
cards.noteEn: The subjunctive is the special verb form Spanish uses here because the action is a result someone is trying to bring about, not a plain fact. For example, ordinary hace changes to haga, and abre changes to abra. Conseguir changes for the person and time, while que stays unchanged. When the same person does both actions, use the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form instead, as in consigo salir.

example.es: Ana consigue que la puerta se abra.
example.en: Ana manages to get the door to open.

cards.noteEn: Conseguido is the completed-action form of conseguir. With has and a que-clause, it asks whether the listener has managed to bring about another result.

example.en: Have you managed to get it to work?

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links conseguir to an action by another actor
cards.noteEn: After conseguir, que introduces the action that the person or thing manages to bring about. English often expresses the same link with ‘get ... to’ rather than translating que as a separate word.

example.en: I manage to get Marta to come.

cards.noteEn: Deje is a special form of dejar used after conseguir que because the stopping is a result someone is trying to bring about. Ordinary deja changes to deje.

example.en: I want it to stop raining.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of dejar, then de, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form of a verb is called the infinitive. It usually ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only dejar changes to show who acts and when; the final verb stays in its dictionary form. Keep de in this pattern: dejar alone usually means “to leave” or “to let,” while dejar de + action means to stop doing that action.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone stops doing something?

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links dejar to the activity being stopped
cards.noteEn: De is required between a form of dejar and the following action in the common pattern dejar de hacer algo, ‘to stop doing something.’

cards.answerEn: to go; to work or run
cards.noteEn: Ir normally means “to go.” In ir bien or ir mal, it describes how something works or is going: va bien means “it works” or “it’s going well.”

cards.promptEs: verbo + adjetivo usado para describir el modo
cards.questionEn: How can words such as claro, alto, or profundo describe how an action is done without adding -mente?
cards.answerEn: In certain common combinations, put the describing word after the verb and keep it in its masculine singular form.
cards.noteEn: A word that normally describes a noun can sometimes work like an English -ly word and describe the action instead: hablar claro, volar alto, respirar profundo. It does not change for the person doing the action. This use is conventional, so it cannot be applied freely to every adjective.
In combinations such as ir lento, lento describes how an action or process runs. It stays masculine singular because it describes the action rather than a noun.

cards.answerEn: you can; you are able to
to make; to cause (someone to do something)
cards.noteEn: Hacer followed by que and a changed verb form can mean causing or making another person perform an action. This is a different sense from hacer meaning simply “to do.”

example.es: El ruido hizo que todos salieran.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone makes or gets another person to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of hacer, then que, then the person and the action in a special caused-action form.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” Hacer changes for who causes the action. The later verb uses a special form called the subjunctive because that action is being caused rather than simply reported: llama becomes llame, and cierra becomes cierre.

example.es: Hago que Ana cierre la puerta.
example.en: I make Ana close the door.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; it links hacer to the caused action
cards.noteEn: After hacer que, the later action uses its special caused-action form.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks sincronizarse, to synchronize
cards.noteEn: Se presents the program as becoming synchronized with something else rather than directly synchronizing an object.
Sincronice is the special form of sincronizar used after hacer que because synchronization is the result being caused. Ordinary sincroniza changes to sincronice.

example.es: Haz que el reloj se sincronice.

cards.noteEn: Nuestro changes to nuestros before more than one masculine or mixed-gender thing. The ending matches what is owned, not the people who own it.

cards.questionEn: How do you choose the Spanish form of ‘our’ before a noun?
cards.answerEn: Choose nuestro, nuestra, nuestros, or nuestras to match the gender and number of what is owned.
cards.noteEn: The form matches the owned noun, not the owners. Use nuestro before one masculine thing, nuestra before one feminine thing, nuestros before masculine or mixed plural things, and nuestras before feminine plural things.

cards.promptEs: una nueva persona o cosa · una persona o cosa nueva
cards.questionEn: What difference can the position of nuevo make?
cards.answerEn: Before the person or thing, nuevo often means newly added or newly in that role; after it, nuevo more often stresses that the thing itself is brand-new.
cards.noteEn: Nuevo changes to nueva, nuevos, or nuevas to match what it describes. Una nueva compañera usually means someone who has recently become a coworker or classmate. Una mesa nueva more often means a newly made or unused table. Context can blur the contrast, so this is a common tendency rather than an absolute rule.
Here móviles stands by itself as the plural noun for mobile or cell phones, with teléfonos understood.

example.en: The new cell phones last longer.
